title: Post-upgrade concurrency flare debugging notes and quick mitigations
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures an iterative troubleshooting runbook for a specific class of post-upgrade incidents we keep seeing on VPC / on-prem installs: a transient or sustained spike in request concurrency (called a "concurrency flare") that causes high tail latency, request queuing, and sometimes upstream 502/503 errors. It's a working set of hypotheses, quick mitigations, Terraform module toggles, and a short smoke-test checklist to validate a fix before rolling to remaining fleets.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Private deployments (VPC + on-prem) where the runtime was upgraded (serving-runtime or kernel/quantization changes) in the last 24–72 hours.
- A "flare" here means either an unexpected increase in concurrent inflight requests per worker or the same concurrency but much higher CPU/GPU stall time per token.
- Assumes access to customer control plane logs, kube nodes (if k8s), terraform module toggles, and monitoring (Prometheus/Grafana) + application logs.

Common symptoms we've observed (examples):
- sudden increase in 95/99 latency for generate/chat endpoints within 15–60 minutes after rollout
- rate of 502/503 or connection resets from the proxy layer that correlate with the latency spike
- worker pods report high cpu wait or long GC/pinned threads in runtime logs
- GPU utilization low while request latencies rise (indicates CPU-side bottleneck/serialization)
- KV cache miss rate stays high or jump in cache misses during the window
- autoscaler panic scaling (rapid up/down) or inability to scale due to quota

Immediate first-response checklist (fast items, <20 minutes):
1) Pause rollout/stop new traffic to rolled revision: use canary route toggle in console or set traffic-split to 0 for suspect revision.
2) Enable fallback policy to previous model variant (if available) to restore baseline throughput.
3) If running k8s: cordon suspect nodes and/or scale down the new replica set while the previous RS is scaled up. If on VMs: remove instances from LB.
4) Turn on verbose runtime logs for the affected revision (capture at least 10m before increasing sampling).
5) Run quick smoke tests against golden path (see Smoke-test checklist below) to confirm whether mitigation reduced tail latency.

Key investigative queries and commands (copy/paste friendly):
- Prometheus: 5m rate of request inflight per worker/group
  sum by(job) (increase(runtime_requests_inflight[5m]))
- Prometheus: per-pod 99p latency for generate
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, pod))
- Check kube events for preemption/oomkills:
  kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp -n <ns> | tail -n 200
- Inspect node dmesg for PCIe or firmware errors (for on-prem):
  sudo dmesg --ctime | tail -n 200
- Runtime log grep examples (increase patterns when verbose enabled):
  grep -E "(stall|blocked|kv-cache-miss|serialize|oom|failed-to-alloc|timeout)" /var/log/redwood/runtime.log | tail -n 200
- Check KV cache hit-rate over 10m windows (our runtime exposes metrics):
  rate(kvcache_hits_total[10m]) / rate(kvcache_requests_total[10m])

Hypotheses (ordered by frequency observed):
A) Runtime scheduling regression: new kernel changed async scheduling and created serialization points; throughput drops despite low GPU usage.
B) TF module/VM sizing mismatch: nodes created during upgrade have different CPU/GPU driver/firmware combos or wrong instance types (e.g., compute-optimized vs memory-optimized) due to a variable/typo in terraform modules.
C) Autoflush/IO change in new runtime causes increased CPU stalls on logging or checkpoint operations (sync writes on hot path).
D) KV cache invalidation bug: upgrade triggers eviction threshold change or version mismatch causing repeated cache repopulation.
E) Autoscaler miscalculation: HPA/scale controller thresholds misinterpreting new metrics name/labels so it underprovisions.

Quick mitigations mapped to hypotheses (pick immediate relevant ones):
- For A (scheduling): revert to previous runtime image (fast rollback) or set runtime env var REDWOOD_RUNTIME_ASYNC=off to force legacy scheduler for the rolled revision. Use this as a canary patch.
- For B (terraform mismatch): check TF plan/last-apply for differences in instance_type, gpu_driver_version, AMI id. If wrong, patch TF var and run a targeted apply (or replace single node via instance lifecycle).
- For C (IO stalls): switch log-level to warn and redirect heavy logging to ephemeral volume. If checkpointing frequency changed, set REDWOOD_CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL to previous value.
- For D (kv cache): set RUNTIME_KV_CACHE_MODE=read-through and increase KVCACHE_CAPACITY temporarily, or invalidate cache gracefully on a single instance then watch hit rate.
- For E (autoscaler): toggle autoscaler to manual target replicas until a fix is validated. Set min_replicas to a safe baseline.

Terraform module notes (practical toggles to patch quickly):
- var.node_labels and var.instance_type: common mistake is using a templated var name like var.worker_prefix resulting in wrong sku. Always inspect the last plan: terraform show -json tfplan.binary | jq '.resource_changes[] | select(.address | contains("aws_instance"))'
- module.gpu_drivers.version: some upgrades require exact driver pinning. Add a temporary override var.gpu_driver_pin to the second-tier TF module and run apply on the node pool module only.
- module.boot_volume.iops: on some on-prem thin-provisioned volumes a spike in iops during upgrade caused OS-level stalls; consider moving to provisioned IOPS or throttling background jobs.
- Use lifecycle.replace_on_change for critical label changes to prevent mixed fleets. Example: lifecycle { replace_on_change = ["tags"] }

Rollback vs roll-forward decision matrix (quick):
- Rollback if: baseline traffic is degraded >20% P95/P99, error rate >1% sustained for >10 minutes, no safe mitigation available in <30 minutes.
- Roll-forward if: issue is known and careful config change (env var or TF var) can be applied to the current revision and validated on canary within 20–30 minutes.
- Always prefer targeted rollback to the previous model revision rather than full infra rollback when the problem is runtime-only.

Post-fix validation smoke-test checklist (run after mitigation, expected PASS criteria in parentheses):
1) Golden request path (small chat completion) 200x sequential (median latency < baseline + 15%, 99p < baseline + 30%).
2) Burst test: 50 clients concurrently hitting chat/generate for 120s (no queue growth, no 5xx). (PASS: max inflight per worker within expected range, errors <= baseline+0.1%).
3) KV cache health: hit-rate >= baseline - 5% and cache population rate stable.
4) GPU utilization sanity: GPUs not idle while CPU not pinned (indicates proper offload).
5) Autoscaler behaviour: if in use, verify that scale-up occurs within configured SLO and no oscillation for 10 minutes.
6) Logs: no repeated "serialize" or "blocked" stack traces; no repeated OOM or allocation failures.

Notes on data capture for postmortem (collect before reset):
- runtime logs (10m before incident start to 20m after mitigation), kube events, node-level syslog/dmesg, kernel oops if any, Prometheus TSDB snapshot for the incident window (use remote_read snapshot or export grafana dashboard JSON panel), terraform state at time of last apply, list of nodes/instances & exact AMI/image id.

Communication template for customers during flare (concise):
- Subject: Incident: increased latency after runtime upgrade – mitigation in progress
- Body bullets: what happened, who/when triggered rollout, immediate mitigation (traffic shifted to previous revision / autoscaler adjusted), ETA for full resolution (we expect fix in 1–2 hours), what we will do next (collect logs, rollback/patch), contact channel.

Follow-up items (post-incident):
- Add canary workload that simulates our largest sequence lengths and concurrency patterns to the upgrade pipeline (blocking metric for rollout).
- Add preflight TF plan validation that checks instance_type/driver pins vs. allowed SKU list.
- Add a runtime feature-flag gating any kernel scheduling changes to be off by default for private deploys, enabled only after canary pass.
- Improve observability: add a dedicated metric for per-request CPU wait time and queue length exported with pod labels.

Appendix: helpful snippets and expected outputs
- quick cache hit query (PromQL):
  sum(rate(kvcache_hits_total[5m])) by (deployment) / sum(rate(kvcache_requests_total[5m])) by (deployment)
  (expect 0.6-0.95 on baseline customer workloads)
- quick pod log tail: kubectl -n <ns> logs deployment/runtime-deployment -c runtime --since=10m | grep -E "(blocked|stall|kv-cache-miss)"
- terraform show diff for node pool: terraform plan -target=module.node_pool -out=tfplan && terraform show -json tfplan | jq '.resource_changes[] | select(.address|test("node_pool|instance"))'

If you are working this incident, add a short timeline note at the top of the doc with timestamps and your name. This doc should evolve into the canonical postmortem fragment for this failure class.

Open questions we still need to answer (research tasks):
- Why do some customer KV cache workloads amplify the scheduling regression while others don't? (difference in prefix reuse distribution?)
- Can we add a small synthetic workload to the control plane that exercises the most common prefix reuse patterns during canaries?
